results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No. Phasing in does not cause a permanent to enter the battlefield; it merely changes the permanent's status from "phased out" to "phased in." Because no zone change occurs, zone-change triggers—including enters-the-battlefield abilities—do not trigger when a permanent phases in. This is explicitly stated in the phasing rules: "Zone-change triggers don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out" [702.26d]. Enters-the-battlefield abilities are a type of zone-change trigger [603.6a].

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text: When an attacking creature has both trample and deathtouch, the deathtouch ability changes what counts as lethal damage for the purpose of trample. Normally, lethal damage equals the blocker's toughness. However, rule 702.2c says that any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered lethal damage for determining excess damage. So, when you assign combat damage with a trample/deathtouch attacker, you only need to assign 1 damage to each blocking creature to satisfy the lethal damage requirement. All remaining damage can then be assigned to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle (as per trample's normal rules in 702.19b). The blocker will still be destroyed later as a state-based action due to deathtouch (rule 704.5h), but that doesn't affect the damage assignment step.

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text: Yes, storm is a triggered ability. According to rule 702.40a, storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack. As a triggered ability on the stack, it is not a spell, so it can't be countered by effects that only counter spells. However, rule 113.9 states that triggered abilities on the stack can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. So storm can be countered, but only by something like Stifle or Disallow, not by a simple Counterspell.

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text: No, you cannot include a card with a hybrid mana symbol in a Commander deck if your commander's color identity doesn't contain all the colors of that symbol. A hybrid mana symbol like {R/G} is both red and green (rule 107.4e), so the card's color identity includes both colors (rule 903.4f). Rule 903.5c states that a card can be in a Commander deck only if every color in its color identity is also found in the color identity of the deck's commander. If your commander is mono-red, its color identity is only red, and a card with {R/G} has green in its color identity, making it illegal.

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to the untap step. During the untap step, no player receives priority, so you cannot cast spells or activate abilities. Any abilities that trigger during the untap step are held and put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority, which is usually during the upkeep step.

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text: Yes, creatures are still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step. The definition of an attacking creature states it remains an attacking creature until it's removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first. The combat phase doesn't end until after the end of combat step concludes; rule 511.3 specifies that creatures are removed from combat as soon as the end of combat step ends. Since the step itself is still part of the combat phase, attacking creatures retain that status throughout the step (unless they were already removed from combat earlier).

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text: No, you do not cast lands. Lands are **played** as a special action that doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to. They are never spells. Even if a card is both a land and another card type (like an artifact land), it can only be played as a land, not cast as a spell. Lands also have no mana cost, so they are simply put onto the battlefield without paying any costs.

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text: Yes, you can sacrifice an evoked creature before its evoke triggered ability resolves. The evoke ability is a normal triggered ability that goes on the stack when the creature enters [702.74a]. After it's put on the stack, players receive priority and can respond with instants or activated abilities [603.3d]. If you sacrifice the creature in response (for example, to an exploit ability or any other sacrifice outlet), the creature leaves the battlefield. When the evoke trigger later resolves, it instructs you to sacrifice that creature, but since it's no longer on the battlefield, the sacrifice can't be performed and the trigger does nothing. The evoke trigger doesn't target, so it isn't countered; it simply resolves with no effect.

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text: Yes, losing all abilities includes keyword abilities. Rule 702.1 defines keyword abilities as a type of ability—they are simply common abilities that are listed by name rather than spelled out in full. Rule 113.10b states that an effect that removes an ability will say the object “loses” that ability, and an effect that says “lose all abilities” removes every ability the object has, including keyword abilities like flying, first strike, or triggered abilities. Rule 603.6b explicitly illustrates this: if an effect reads “All creatures lose all abilities” and a creature with an enters-the-battlefield triggered ability enters the battlefield, that triggered ability won’t trigger because it is lost the moment the creature enters. Rule 113.2a further confirms that even simple statements like “This creature can’t block” are abilities, so any keyword ability is an ability and is removed by a blanket loss of all abilities.

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes, you can draw cards even if you're already at your maximum hand size. The rules explicitly state that a player may have any number of cards in their hand [402.2]. The maximum hand size only matters during your cleanup step, when you must discard down to that number [514.1, 703.4n]. There is no rule that prevents you from drawing cards while your hand is already at or above the maximum.

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text: When a planeswalker has 0 loyalty counters, its loyalty is 0 (rule 306.5c). As a state-based action, that planeswalker is put into its owner's graveyard (rules 306.9, 122.1e, 704.5i). There is no concept of negative loyalty counters; a planeswalker's loyalty is simply the number of loyalty counters on it, and counters cannot be negative.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text: No. The term "dies" is defined only for creatures and planeswalkers. A non-creature artifact that is put into a graveyard from the battlefield is not considered to have died, even though it moved from the battlefield to the graveyard.

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text: When you are required to draw a card and your library is empty, you attempt to draw but there are no cards to draw. This causes you to lose the game the next time state-based actions are checked (i.e., before any player receives priority). This is a state-based action defined by rule 704.5b, and it applies whether you're drawing one card or multiple cards (rule 104.3c). The loss isn't immediate—it waits until state-based actions are next performed, so no player can respond between the failed draw and the loss.

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
The combat phase has five steps in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat. If no attackers are declared, the declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped. If any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike, there are two combat damage steps instead of one.

As the defending player (the nonactive player in a two‑player game, or one of the defending players in multiplayer), you receive priority in each step after the active player (the attacking player) has passed priority. Specifically:
- At the start of each step, any turn‑based actions occur (e.g., choosing a defending player in some multiplayer games at the beginning of combat, assigning combat damage in the combat damage step). Then triggered abilities go on the stack. Then the active player gets priority. Once the active player passes, you get priority.
- This pattern repeats in every step: beginning of combat, declare attackers (after attackers are declared), declare blockers (after blockers are declared), each combat damage step (after damage is assigned and dealt), and end of combat.

So you can act when you have priority during any of these steps, always after the attacking player has had the chance to act first.

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a mana ability. A mana ability is an activated or triggered ability that could create mana and, by definition, does not use the stack. Activated mana abilities resolve immediately after they are activated, and triggered mana abilities resolve immediately after the mana ability that triggered them, without waiting for priority. Because they never go on the stack, they can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to.

results.question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a cost being paid. A cost is an action or payment necessary to take another action (rule 118.1). Paying a cost is not an independent event that uses the stack; it is a step within a larger process such as casting a spell (rules 118.2, 601.2g–h), activating an ability, or declaring attackers/blockers (rules 508.1j, 509.1f). During these processes, no player receives priority to cast spells or activate non-mana abilities—only mana abilities may be activated when required (rule 601.2g). Once the spell or ability is fully cast/activated and placed on the stack, players can respond to that spell or ability, not to the cost payment itself.

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text:
Layers are the system that determines the order in which continuous effects are applied to an object's characteristics. The game starts with the actual object (printed card or token definition) and then applies all applicable continuous effects in a strict sequence of layers, from layer 1 to layer 7. Within some layers, there are sublayers that further order effects. The process is automatic and instantaneous.

The layers, in order, are:
- **Layer 1:** Rules and effects that modify copiable values. This includes copy effects and merging with permanents (layer 1a), and other copiable effects like "as . . . enters" abilities that set power/toughness [613.1a, 613.2a]. After layer 1, the object's characteristics are its copiable values [613.2c].
- **Layer 2:** Control-changing effects (not detailed in the provided rules, but mentioned in examples [613.6]).
- **Layer 3:** Text-changing effects [613.1c].
- **Layer 4:** Type-changing effects (card type, subtype, supertype) [613.1d].
- **Layer 5:** Color-changing effects [613.1e].
- **Layer 6:** Ability-adding/removing effects, keyword counters, and effects that say an object can't have an ability [613.1f].
- **Layer 7:** Power- and toughness-changing effects. This layer has sublayers applied in order: 7a (characteristic-defining abilities that define power/toughness [613.4a]), 7b (effects that set power/toughness to a specific value), and 7c (effects that modify power/toughness without setting, like +1/+1 counters or +X/+X effects) [613.5, 613.6].

Within each layer or sublayer, effects are normally applied in timestamp order (the order they were created). However, if one effect depends on another—meaning applying the other would change the text, existence, or what the first effect applies to or does—the dependency system overrides timestamp order, and the independent effect is applied first [613.8, 613.8a]. Characteristic-defining abilities are applied before other effects in layers 2–6 [613.3].

If an effect has parts that apply in different layers, each part is applied in its appropriate layer, and the effect continues to apply to the same set of objects even if the ability generating it is removed [613.6]. The entire layer system is continually and automatically maintained by the game, so any change to an object's characteristics is immediately reflected [613.5].

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text: The legend rule is a state-based action that prevents a player from controlling two or more legendary permanents with the same name. Whenever state-based actions are checked (right before a player would receive priority), if a player controls multiple legendary permanents that share a name, that player must choose one to keep. All the others are put into their owners' graveyards. This happens automatically and doesn't use the stack. The rule applies to any permanent with the supertype "legendary," including planeswalkers (which were errata'd to be legendary).

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text: Your creature dies the next time state-based actions are checked after the lethal damage is marked on it. This happens right after the spell, ability, or combat damage step that dealt the damage finishes, before any player receives priority. The creature is destroyed as a state-based action (rule 704.5g) and put into its owner's graveyard immediately; this doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to.

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text: No, you cannot cast your commander from exile. The Commander rules only allow you to cast your commander from the command zone [903.8]. If your commander is in exile, you have the option to put it into the command zone as a state-based action [903.9a], but you cannot cast it directly from exile unless another effect specifically allows you to cast spells from exile.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text:
The cleanup step is the second and final step of the ending phase. During this step, two things happen in order: first, the active player discards down to their maximum hand size if they have too many cards. Immediately after that, all damage is removed from permanents and all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end simultaneously. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack.

Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated. However, if any state-based actions would be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack (including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”), the game performs those state-based actions, puts those triggered abilities on the stack, and then the active player gets priority. Players may then cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins. If no state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting, the step ends without any player getting priority.

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text: State-based actions are checked automatically whenever a player would get priority (rules 704.3, 117.5). This occurs after turn-based actions at the beginning of steps and phases (rule 703.3), after spells and abilities resolve, and during the cleanup step if any state-based actions would be performed (rule 514.3a). Additionally, they are checked during the resolution of effects that end the combat phase (rule 724.2c) or end the turn (rule 724.1c), without players receiving priority. State-based actions happen automatically and are not controlled by any player (rule 704.2, 117.2d).

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text: You can concede the game at any time. This is a special action that doesn't use the stack and happens immediately. It doesn't matter whose turn it is, whether you have priority, or even if another player controls your turn — you can always concede. The only exception is that a player controlling you can't force you to concede; the choice is always yours.

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text: The active player is simply the player whose turn it is. In a standard game, that's the person currently taking their turn. In a game using the shared team turns option, all players on the active team are considered active players (see rule 805.4a), and if an ability refers to "the active player," its controller chooses which specific active player it means (rule 805.9).

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: When a nonactive player casts a spell, that player receives priority immediately afterward. This is because rule 117.3c states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward. So the nonactive player who just cast the spell gets priority first, before the active player or any other player.

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: When the active player casts a spell, they receive priority again immediately afterward. This is because rule 117.3c states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Since the active player must have priority to cast the spell in the first place, they are the one who gets priority first after casting it.

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text: Yes, you can hold priority. After you cast a spell, if you had priority before casting it, you receive priority again immediately [601.2i]. This is also stated in the general rule: the player who had priority when they cast a spell gets priority afterward [117.3c]. So you may cast another spell (or activate an ability) right away without passing priority to your opponent.

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text:
Lore counters are placed on Sagas in two distinct situations:

1. **As the Saga enters the battlefield.**  
   - If the Saga **does not have read ahead**, it enters with exactly one lore counter (rule 714.3a).  
   - If the Saga **has read ahead**, its controller chooses a number between 1 and its final chapter number, and it enters with that many lore counters (rule 714.3b, 702.155b). Both are replacement effects that modify how the permanent enters.

2. **During each of its controller’s precombat main phases.**  
   - Immediately after a player’s precombat main phase begins, that player puts one lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities (rules 714.3c, 703.4f, 505.4). This is a turn-based action that doesn’t use the stack.

No other timing for adding lore counters is provided in the given rules; additional counters would require specific card effects not covered here.

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is a special kind of triggered ability created by a spell or ability as it resolves, by a replacement effect, or by a static ability that lets a player take an action. It waits for a future event and uses the words “when,” “whenever,” or “at” (though those words don’t usually start the ability). Unlike ordinary triggered abilities, a delayed triggered ability triggers only once—the next time its trigger event happens—unless it has a stated duration like “this turn.” If multiple events occur simultaneously, the controller chooses which one causes it to trigger. The ability is created during the resolution of the effect that generates it, and it won’t trigger until after it’s been created, even if the trigger event happened just before. Delayed triggered abilities are one-shot effects that instruct a player to do something later in the game.

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes, non-permanent spells (instants and sorceries) can have abilities. Rule 113.3a defines **spell abilities** as the text on an instant or sorcery spell that is followed as instructions while it resolves—unless that text is an activated, triggered, or static ability that fits the criteria in rule 113.6. Rule 113.6 further states that abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function only while that object is on the stack, confirming that such spells can possess abilities (including activated, triggered, or static ones) that operate on the stack.

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text: Yes, you can activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. Split second explicitly allows players to activate mana abilities (and take special actions) even though it normally prevents casting spells and activating non-mana abilities. This is stated directly in rule 702.61b, and rule 702.61a clarifies that the restriction only applies to non-mana abilities.

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text: Counterspell resolves first because it's the topmost object on the stack (rule 608.1). When it resolves, it counters Divination, which means Divination is removed from the stack, doesn't resolve, and none of its effects occur—it goes to its owner's graveyard (rule 701.6a). Divination never gets to resolve.

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: Because Vampire Nighthawk has deathtouch, any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to it is considered lethal damage for trample purposes (rule 702.2c). Your Charging Rhino (a 4/4 with trample) only needs to assign 1 damage to the Nighthawk to satisfy the lethal damage requirement. The remaining 3 damage can then be assigned to the defending player as excess damage (rule 702.19b, 120.4a).

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text:
Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggers when you cast the noncreature spell off cascade, and that trigger resolves **before** the cascaded spell does.

Here's the sequence:
1. You cast Shardless Agent. Its cascade ability triggers and goes on the stack above Shardless Agent.
2. Cascade resolves first (Shardless Agent ruling #1). During that resolution, you exile cards and may cast the exiled noncreature spell without paying its mana cost. Casting that spell follows the normal steps (601.2a–i), and at the moment the spell becomes cast, prowess triggers (702.108a, 601.2i).
3. Because the casting happens during the resolution of cascade, the prowess trigger waits to be put on the stack. The example in rule 704.4 shows that abilities triggering during a spell's resolution go on the stack after that spell finishes resolving. Here, the resolving spell is the cascade ability, so the prowess trigger is put on the stack after cascade finishes.
4. Once cascade is done, the stack contains (from bottom to top): Shardless Agent spell, the cascaded spell, and then the prowess trigger. Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2 confirms that prowess goes on the stack on top of the spell that caused it and resolves before that spell.
5. Therefore, the prowess trigger resolves first, giving Monastery Swiftspear +1/+1 until end of turn. Only then does the cascaded spell resolve.

So prowess triggers and resolves before the cascaded spell.

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text: Yes. The Grizzly Bears is a 2/2 creature with 2 damage marked on it. Damage marked on a creature remains until the cleanup step [120.6]. Whenever a player would get priority, the game checks state-based actions [704.3]. One of those actions destroys a creature with toughness greater than 0 if the total damage marked on it is greater than or equal to its toughness [704.5g]. After you cast Lightning Bolt, the active player would get priority, so state-based actions are checked first. The game sees a 2/2 with 2 damage marked—lethal damage—and destroys the Bears. Only then would Lightning Bolt try to resolve, but its target is already gone.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text:
Both triggers fire at the moment the upkeep step begins. According to rule 500.6, abilities that trigger “at the beginning of” a step trigger when that step begins. Rule 603.2b confirms that whenever a game event matches a triggered ability’s trigger event, the ability automatically triggers. So your Phyrexian Arena and your opponent’s beginning-of-upkeep ability trigger simultaneously as the upkeep starts.

Before you (the active player) get priority, those triggers must be put on the stack. Rule 503.1a says that any abilities that triggered at the beginning of the upkeep are put onto the stack before the active player receives priority. The order they go on the stack is governed by rule 603.3b: first, each player in APNAP order (active player, then non-active player) puts their triggered abilities on the stack in any order they choose. Since you are the active player, you put your Phyrexian Arena trigger on the stack first. Then your opponent puts their trigger on the stack. Because the stack resolves from the top down, the opponent’s trigger will end up on top and resolve before your Arena trigger. You do not get to choose the relative order between your trigger and the opponent’s trigger; APNAP order dictates that the non-active player’s trigger goes on top. After both triggers are on the stack, you receive priority (rule 117.3a).

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text: When you cast a sorcery with buyback and pay the buyback cost, the spell gains a replacement effect: as it resolves, instead of going to the graveyard, it goes to its owner's hand (rule 702.27a). Fork creates a copy of that spell on the stack. The copy is not a card; it's a spell copy that exists only on the stack (rule 707.10). The copy inherits all decisions made for the original, including the fact that the buyback cost was paid. However, as Fork's ruling #8 explicitly states: "If you copy a spell for which Buyback has been paid, you get nothing back since the copied spell does not have a card to give you." So when the copy resolves, there is no physical card to return to your hand. After the copy resolves, it ceases to exist as a state-based action (rule 704.5e). The original spell, being an actual card, returns to your hand as normal. Therefore, only one card—the original sorcery—ends up in your hand.

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No, you don't get a token. The manifested card is Lightning Bolt, an instant — a nonpermanent card. Mimic Vat's own ruling explicitly states: "If the creature that dies is an instant or sorcery card that's been manifested, Mimic Vat may have a nonpermanent card exiled. You can't create a token that's a copy of a nonpermanent card. No token is created in this case." So even though Lightning Bolt is exiled with Mimic Vat, the activated ability will not create a token.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text: Yes, both exiled creatures return. Fiend Hunter's two abilities are linked: the enters-the-battlefield ability exiles a creature, and the leaves-the-battlefield ability returns "the exiled card." When you copy the exile ability with Lithoform Engine, the copy is also linked to the same return ability. As a result, the return ability sees all cards exiled by both the original and the copy, and returns each of them to the battlefield under its owner's control.

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text: No, the exiled creature does not return. Banishing Light's ability exiles the creature "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield." Phasing out does not cause a permanent to leave the battlefield (rule 702.26d), so the condition for returning the exiled card is not met. Moreover, a specific ruling for Teferi's Protection (ruling #21) explicitly states that one-shot effects waiting for "until [this] leaves the battlefield" won't happen when a permanent phases out. The creature remains in exile.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text:
Yes, your opponent can target Emrakul with Counterspell while it's on the stack. Protection from instants only functions while Emrakul is on the battlefield; on the stack it's a spell and can be targeted by instant spells like Counterspell. This is explicitly stated in Emrakul's rulings: "Protection abilities only apply while the object with the ability is on the battlefield. Notably, Emrakul may be the target of a spell that targets it while on the stack, such as Syncopate." [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2]

Even if Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, you will still control the opponent's next turn. The "When you cast this spell" ability is a triggered ability that goes on the stack after Emrakul is cast (rule 601.2i). It is a separate object from the Emrakul spell itself. Counterspell only counters the spell, not the triggered ability (rule 113.9). The trigger will resolve after Counterspell, regardless of whether Emrakul is still on the stack, so you gain control of the targeted opponent during their next turn and they take an extra turn afterward.

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text:
Yes, Valki, God of Lies is a legal cascade hit. Cascade exiles cards until it finds a nonland card with mana value less than the cascade spell's mana value. While in exile, a modal double-faced card like Valki // Tibalt can be evaluated using any face that fits the criteria (Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16). The front face, Valki, is a nonland card with mana value 2, so if your cascade spell's mana value is 3 or greater, the card qualifies as a hit.

Once you've exiled it, cascade lets you cast that card without paying its mana cost, but only if the resulting spell's mana value is less than the cascade spell's mana value. If you choose to cast the back face, Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor, its mana value is 7. You can cast Tibalt for free only if your cascade spell's mana value is 8 or higher. If the cascade spell's mana value is 7 or less, you cannot cast Tibalt this way, but you could still cast Valki (mana value 2) for free, provided that value is less than the cascade spell's mana value.
citations: [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16]

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You control **one** of your opponent’s turns (their next turn), and they get **two extra turns** after that turn. You **do** get a second Emrakul (a token copy), but the legend rule will make you put one into your graveyard. Copying the Emrakul spell **does not** give you another control‑a‑turn trigger.

Here’s the breakdown:

1. **Copying the cast trigger** – You use Lithoform Engine’s first ability to copy the triggered ability “When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player’s next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn.” The copy is put on the stack and you may choose new targets [707.10]. In a typical two‑player game, both the original and the copy target the same opponent. When they resolve, the last one to resolve (the copy) overwrites the earlier control effect, so you control that opponent’s next turn. However, each ability still creates an extra turn for that opponent [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14]. Result: you control one turn, and the opponent takes two extra turns after it.

2. **Copying the Emrakul spell** – You use Lithoform Engine’s third ability to copy the Emrakul permanent spell on the stack. The copy is put on the stack as a spell, but it is **not cast** [707.10]. When it resolves, it becomes a token with all the characteristics of Emrakul [111.13]. You now have two legendary Emrakul permanents; the legend rule (a state‑based action) will force you to choose one to keep and put the other into its owner’s graveyard. So you do get a second Emrakul, albeit briefly.

3. **No extra cast trigger** – Because the copy of the Emrakul spell was not cast, its “When you cast this spell” ability does not trigger. Lithoform Engine’s ruling confirms that creating a copy on the stack won’t cause cast triggers [Lithoform Engine ruling #6]. The only control‑a‑turn triggers you get are from the original cast and the copy of that trigger you made with the Engine’s first ability.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text: Yes, you get two tokens. When you activate Mimic Vat's second ability, it goes on the stack. You then copy that ability with Lithoform Engine's first ability. The copy is put onto the stack as a separate object (rule 707.10b). The copy has the same source as the original ability—the same Mimic Vat (Lithoform Engine ruling #0). When the copy resolves, it creates a token that's a copy of whatever card is currently exiled with that Mimic Vat (Mimic Vat ruling #4). The original ability also resolves and creates a token the same way. Both tokens are created, so you end up with two tokens that are copies of the exiled creature card.

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0, the mana cost is {G}{G}. Your cost reducer of {1} is generic mana reduction, which can only reduce generic mana components (rule 118.7a). Since the cost has no generic mana, the reduction does nothing, leaving the total cost at {G}{G}. Trinisphere then sees a mana component of two mana, which is less than three, so it forces the spell to cost three mana to cast (Trinisphere ruling #0). The final cost becomes {1}{G}{G}, and you create zero tokens.

For value, you should choose X=2. With X=2, the mana cost is {2}{G}{G}. The {1} reduction reduces the generic part to {1}, making the total cost {1}{G}{G} (three mana). Trinisphere does not apply because the mana component is not less than three. You pay {1}{G}{G} and get two 1/1 tokens. X=1 would also cost {1}{G}{G} after Trinisphere but only give one token, and X=3 costs {2}{G}{G} for three tokens, so X=2 gives the best token-to-mana ratio under these conditions.

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text: Yes, you can target Grist, the Hunger Tide with Animate Dead while it's in your graveyard. Grist's static ability makes it a 1/1 Insect creature card in addition to its other types as long as it's not on the battlefield, so it's a legal target for Animate Dead's "enchant creature card in a graveyard." When Animate Dead's enters-the-battlefield trigger resolves, it returns Grist to the battlefield. Once on the battlefield, Grist is only a planeswalker—it stops being a creature. Animate Dead then tries to attach to Grist, but it can't legally enchant a noncreature permanent. As a state-based action, Animate Dead is put into its owner's graveyard. This causes Animate Dead's delayed triggered ability ("When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it") to trigger. When that trigger resolves, you sacrifice Grist. The net result is that Grist ends up back in your graveyard and Animate Dead is also in your graveyard.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text: Yes, Skullbriar keeps the four +1/+1 counters. Its ability says counters remain on it as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library, so they stay on it through the graveyard, command zone, stack, and battlefield. However, Doubling Season does **not** double those counters. Skullbriar's ruling explicitly states that the counters that remain on it as it changes zones aren't "placed" on it, so effects like Doubling Season won't affect them.

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No, you do not lose the game during that extra turn. The delayed triggered ability from Final Fortune ("At the beginning of that turn's end step, you lose the game") never triggers because the end step is skipped when you end the turn early. However, the ability isn't gone—it will trigger at the beginning of the next turn's end step instead. So you'll lose the game at that point unless you can prevent it.

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text: You choose what Clone copies as it enters the battlefield, during the resolution of the Clone spell. This is a replacement effect (rule 616.1c) that modifies how Clone enters. You may choose any creature already on the battlefield (Clone ruling #2), or choose nothing to have it enter as a 0/0. The choice is not a target (Clone ruling #0) and is made immediately before Clone enters; no player gets priority to respond to the choice itself. Opponents can respond to the Clone spell while it's on the stack, before it resolves, but they won't know what you'll pick. After Clone enters as a copy, any enters-the-battlefield triggers go on the stack and can be responded to normally.

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text: You get three lands total. The original Flooded Strand ability and the two copies each resolve independently. Each one instructs you to search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle. Because each ability includes its own shuffle instruction, they are separate search events and are not combined into a single search under rule 701.23h. The copies don't require you to pay any costs again, and the original Flooded Strand is already sacrificed, so you simply perform the search three times.
